title: Thesis, argument and the essay
note: A thesis states an essay's main claim: specific, arguable and supportable. Each body paragraph develops one point with evidence and explains how that evidence supports the claim. A strong argument answers the best opposing view fairly, and its conclusion shows why the claim matters instead of repeating it.

read.title: Anatomy of an argument
text: An argumentative essay begins with a thesis, a claim that a reasonable person could dispute. "Exercise is healthy" is not a thesis, because almost no one denies it. "High schools should require a daily physical education class" is, because thoughtful people disagree. A good thesis is also narrow enough to defend in the space available.

Each body paragraph then supports one reason for the claim. A reason alone is not enough; it needs evidence, such as data, examples or expert testimony, and it needs explanation. The writer must show how the evidence leads to the claim. In the Toulmin model this connecting logic is called the warrant.

Strong arguments also face their opposition. A writer who ignores the best objection looks either uninformed or evasive. A writer who states it fairly, concedes what is true in it, and then answers it earns the reader's trust. Distorting an opponent's view to make it easy to knock down is the straw man fallacy, and careful readers notice it.
Finally, the conclusion should not merely repeat the thesis. It should show what the argument adds up to and why it matters.

q.q: Why is "Exercise is healthy" not a good thesis?
In the Toulmin model, what is the warrant?
o: The logic connecting evidence to the claim

q.q: According to the reading, how does a writer earn trust when facing objections?
o: By restating the thesis more forcefully
By stating the best objection fairly and answering it
